It has been said that when the people were asking for bread the government gave them a stone. There was the construction of a wharf, sewer works, sidewalks, and pillars for a bridge. A resolution was passed by the school board in my home town of Riviere du Loup asking for an expenditure of relief moneys to build schools. I do not wish to speak further, but should like to quote from Montesquieu, the great French philosopher, who wrote about the organization of the state. The following are his words:
In a free state, every man who is supposed a free agent ought to be concerned in his own government; therefore the legislative should reside in the whole body of the people or their representatives. The political liberty of the subject is a tranquillity of mind, arising from the opinion each person has of his safety. In order to have this liberty, it is requisite the government be so constituted that one man need not be afraid of another. When the power of making laws and the power of executing them are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty, because apprehensions may arise, lest the same monarch or Senate should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner.
A great British parliamentarian, Charles James Fox, on one occasion uttered these memorable words:
We are compelled to own that the democratic form of government gives a power of which no other form is capable. Why? Because it incorporates every man with the state. Because it arouses everything that belongs to the soul, as well as to the body of man. Because it makes every individual feel that he is fighting for himself; that it is his owm cause, his own safety, his owm dignity, on the face of the earth, that he is asserting.
Then may I quote Byron:
Freedom's battle, once begun,
Bequeath'd by bleeding sire to son,
Tho' baffled oft, is ever won.
In my part of the country, Mr. Speaker, we do not complain of the fact that the federal director of unemployment wrote us for information with respect to the best way of helping the unemployed; but we do complain that no notice was taken of the representations which we made to him. Why should he object that we sent to him requests for works that came under provincial jurisdiction when at the time no order in council had been passed designating the relative jurisdiction in the matter of the federal and provincial authorities? I am confident that every member of this house took the same course-gave the director of unemployment relief all available information in reply to his request. My grievance is that in my constituency certain selfish people were too ready to keep all they possibly could for themselves without giving any consideration whatever to their need}' brothers. May I tell the right [Mr. Pouliot.}
hon. Prime Minister and the members of his government that I am convinced they are well-disposed towards our people who are suffering at the present time, and I cannot believe they are so hard-hearted as to shut their eyes to the misery of the unemployed. Therefore I would advise them to take the right means to help those people. We on this side of the house do not pretend to be infallible, neither do we think our friends opposite never make mistakes, but I believe we are all animated by good will towards the unemployed, and we are here at great personal sacrifice to do our best to relieve their sufferings as far as possible. That is why we offer our very hearty cooperation to the government, and in discussing matters affecting unemployment we do so not to obstruct, but to keep the government well posted on matters of such vital importance to the country generally.

On behalf of my constituents Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) to the fact that this present bill will not meet their requirements. Last week I had the pleasure of presenting to him a petition from my people to extend relief until the first of June, or, if possible, the first of July. I hope he will give this request his favourable consideration.
On August 7, 1931, in common with other members of the house, I received a letter from the dominion director of unemployment relief asking for information as to steps necessary to give employment to the largest number of people in my constituency. I had copies of the letter made and sent to about thirty municipalities in my riding, and I got the local authorities to cooperate and recommend what works should be undertaken. Those recommendations were transmitted to the minister, but that is the last I heard of them until some months ago, when I found that an agreement bad been arrived at between the federal and the provincial government to assume their respective shares of the cost of certain unemployment relief works. These works are divided into three classes in my constituency. First, we have the ordinary federal public works, but no new undertakings of this class have been started. Secondly, we have provincial public works, part of the cost of which is contributed by the dominion treasury. The third class covers municipal works in which the farmers of my riding are more directly concerned, the cost of which is borne by the dominion, the province and the municipality in certain proportions. The disadvantages of

Unemployment Continuance Act
this latter class of works is that they do not provide sufficient employment. After the elections in 1930 the people expected that the new administration would bring about such an improved state of affairs that there would be no unemployment, that work would be found for everyone, and that the prosperity that had existed so long under the Laurier regime, and again under the Mackenzie King regime, would prevail once more.
Of course, the measures taken now cannot be considered a solution of the problem of unemployment. The people of my riding are disappointed that the promises made to them in 1930 have not been fulfilled, and the closing up of saw mills and other local industries has brought about a condition in my constituency more serious than anything I can remember. I have had the honour of sitting in this house through many sessions- this is my thirty-fifth-and I am sorry to say that I have never seen Canada passing through such an ordeal of depression as now prevails. In the campaign of 1878, when the Mackenzie government was turned out of office because of hard times, the depression was a drop in the bucket compared with the present condition. In 1894 and 1895 we had a similar condition; then Laurier came into office. Now, after twenty or twenty-five years, we seem to agree that the policy inaugurated by Laurier and Fielding was sound. The chief reason for our difficulties at the present time, our financial condition, our railway catastrophe and our unemployment situation, is lack of markets. We have no markets for our products, and that condition has been brought about by increases in the tariff which have closed our markets to the products of other countries and shut our goods out of other markets. Tariffs are barriers to the free intercourse of nations; they must be lowered if we are to have good will between the nations of the world and if prosperity is to return.
When I was elected in 1911 we did not dream we would soon be at war with Germany, but I was here for the special session in August, 1914, and I was proud to pledge the support of my people in that crisis. We had no choice then; we were not asked whether or not we wanted to go to war. War had been declared, and the money for the first, second and third contingents was voted without a dissenting voice. But when the rules of the game were changed and conscription was imposed upon the people, we asked that the question be referred to the people. That request was refused. That was 41761-97J
the second time closure was resorted to in thio house, but now it has become quite a common practice. Probably as our business increases and the time at our disposal decreases, closure will be invoked more often.
I say frankly, Mr. Speaker, that in connection with a question so vitally affecting the people as that of unemployment, it is too bad that an understanding could not have been arrived at between the two political parties. The leader of the opposition declared many times in the name of the party to which I have the honour to belong that we were prepared to give the government all possible assistance if they would follow parliamentary practice. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, who are old parliamentarians, know that this is far removed from ordinary parliamentary procedure; it is something to which we are not accustomed. Though we may have faith in the honesty of the government and may feel sure that this money will be expended in the public interest, there is no limit to the expenditure. The St. Lawrence waterway or anything else might be constructed under this measure. Back in 1837 this same question of taxation without representation came to a head. The governor of that day was surrounded by a council and did not consult the assembly; he simply imposed taxes and spent the money as he saw fit. The people objected; the cry of "no taxation without representation" was kept up for several years, and finally all that we asked was conceded. All we ask now is that the foundation of parliamentary institutions be observed and that the control of public expenditures by the representatives of the people be continued. That is the parliamentary procedure, and it should be followed. Unfortunately it has not been followed; the majority rules, the majority have resorted to closure, and we have had to submit. But let me again call the attention of the government to the fact that they are mistaken if they imagine that by such means as this the difficulty in Canada can be remedied. It will be remedied only when a wiser policy prevails and when we realize that we cannot do business with other nations unless they do business with us. If we break down those barriers and maintain a tariff merely for the purposes of revenue we will be doing something really worth while.
In the old days,' Mr. Speaker, the idea of federal taxation was that it should be indirect collected through customs and excise and so on, but circumstances have changed and the

Unemployment Continuance Act
case has been altered. Now we have a new state of affairs. We are to have a conference, and for the sake of the country I hope that conference may be successful. When the delegates of the British government come here and ask if we will admit from Great Britain cottons, woollen goods, iron and steel and coal, what will be our position? One of the planks of the platform of the Conservative party is protection for cotton and woollen mills, the iron and steel industry and so on. We can get nothing from Great Britain unless we give something in return; we must give a quid pro quo. We will be compelled by the force of circumstances to follow that idea, and then I hope a new light will dawn on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. They may realize then that when England imposed a tariff, that tariff amounted to only ten per cent. The high tariff we have in this country is of no advantage either to the government or to the country; the higher the tariff the smaller the revenue. Our trade has fallen off by about $500,000,000 or $600,000,000 in the last two or three years, something we did not dream could happen in such a short time. We are losing from $500,000 to $1,000,000 a week on our railways; people are unemployed, and we are in a serious condition. As I said before, it is too bad that both political parties could not have agreed to the appointment of a national committee to deal with the situation. There are times in the history of nations, as well as in the history of individuals, when we must get away from parties, and I hope the government will consult the men at the heads of the provincial governments so that before this session closes we may show that we are willing to cooperate and do our share of what must be done.
Let me conclude by again directing the attention of the Minister of Labour to the geographical location of the county of Bona-venture, where the long winter and late spring have made it impossible to carry on the work proposed. No relief has been given there; few of the works have been even started, so if the government persist in handing out money this way they will have to extend this measure far beyond May 1. There is a mayoralty campaign proceeding in the city of Montreal at the present time, and every night speeches are being made by the candidates and their friends. It is being freely predicted that next winter will be the worst in the history of Montreal, with no relief given, with the work on the new station stopped and no new work being commenced.

The condition in which we find ourselves is very bad, and I sympathize with the Prime Minister in his predicament. I hope he will see the wisdom of dropping party lines at a time like this and working with all hon. members of this house in the interests of the whole people.

The Minister of Labour is not in his place, but no doubt other ministers will answer two or three questions I have to ask. At page 28 of the report giving a resume of unemployment relief I find that the city of Sherbrooke was allotted a certain amount of money, and the proportions paid from the federal treasury and out of different moneys are given. At page 65 there is an item, at the bottom of the page, of money spent in Sherbrooke and taken out of unemployment money, but through the Public Works department. Why is this separation made? For what reason has money been spent through the Public Works department and also directly from the unemployment relief fund?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There were made out of the fund direct appropriations which were expended under the control of the Public Works department as public works. Then there were municipal works which were arranged between the province and the municipalities, to which the dominion contributed the proportions that are mentioned in the schedules. The division was arrived at in this way. In Nova Scotia, for instance, where there had been a storm that had swept over a considerable section of the coast, repairs had to be made to wharves, and matters of that kind. In the province of Quebec, as the hon. gentleman will recall, communications were sent to the members, and I am bound to say that if the suggestions had all been given effect to it' would have been rather difficult to conduct government at all. But in a broad and general way Mr. Hereford tabulated them and then the department undertook the construction of the works in question, similar to those that are mentioned here, some of which could be completed by February 29, although others could not. The Department of the Interior had, for example, a grant with respect to national parks, and under

Unemployment Continuance Act
railways and canals there were matters to which reference has been made this afternoon. The dividing line was arbitrarily fixed in one way but not in another; that is to say, such works as it has been the custom of the Public Works department or the Railway department or the Department of the Interior to undertake were undertaken by these departments in connection with unemployment relief, the object being to employ as many people' as possible while work was being carried forward.

The Prime Minister has not exactly got what I am driving at. The money was allotted and the proportions were fixed to be contributed by the city of Sherbrooke, by the federal government and by the provincial authorities, and that money went through the channels of the provincial government; this government did not have it. It went through the provincial government, who approved of the works, and the city of Sherbrooke contributed its share and did the work. At the bottom of page 65 there are indicated certain works done directly from here. I am not going to discuss these items except where they concern my own county, but, as I say, at the bottom of page 65 there is this small item: "Sherbrooke-public building, S742." The point is this. That money was taken out of the public treasury or out of the unemployment fund; but why was it not shown in the estimates in the regular way, charged either to income or to capital through the Public Works department, and not from unemployment moneys? Who is to decide whether the money shall come out of the unemployment fund or through the regular channels of the Public Works department

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I take it that the hon.
gentleman, being a resident of Sherbrooke, will be able to determine whether or not that $742 was for repairs. With respect to a large number of these items, my memory is that reports were asked for from the resident engineers as to what works might reasonably be done to afford employment to casual labourers such as carpenters and men occupied similarly. This $742, if it is like the items I have in mind-the hon. gentleman will be able to speak with authority so far as this item is concerned-would represent work done for the purpose of affording such employment as was possible to men who sometimes might, for instance, repair a sewer or perhaps the outside premises in connection with a public building, or who might do painting. Painting is one bit of work that was done in many instances. The reason it is not in the estimates is that parliament was not in session
at the time the money was expended or when the reports were made; but as I have indicated to the house on many occasions, these items are all represented by vouchers for expenditure, which the auditor general approves, as he does any other item of public expenditure. They could not well be in the estimates because they did not arise until afterwards. The supreme purpose was unemployment relief.

At the last session the Prime Minister told us that in order to relieve distress in the dried-out area and in the agricultural districts of the west, the government proposed a $5,000,000 revolving credit, through a credit association under what is known as the Beatty scheme. Has that scheme been put into operation and has credit been extended to the western farmers? Perhaps the Prime Minister will inform the committee how much has been given out or whether that scheme is in operation at the present time. Is there a report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I told hon. gentlemen, it was not a governmental instrumentality; it was an instrumentality for the public to which the government had made a contribution. A contribution was made through the Canadian National Railways and contributions were made through the Canadian Pacific Railway, the banks and the trust companies to create the fund; but the government has nothing whatever to do with the direction or administration of it. I have not inquired into the matter within the last month or so, but the administration was in charge of a very excellent gentleman as general manager, who at one time, if my memory serves me, was general manager of the Weyburn Securities bank. As to the extent to which their operations were carried on, I cannot say, because I have not the information; it has not been given to us. It is not a governmental instrumentality.

I wish to move a small
amendment if the Prime Minister will accept it; if he does not, I will not press it. In the fifth line of section 1, I would suggest that the word "not" should be deleted and inserted instead after the word "deemed." As the section reads now, it is provided that the act "shall not be deemed to have expired" on a certain date. The dictionary meaning of the word "deemed" is thought, or considered, or assumed, or pretended. While "pretended" is an excessive stressing of the word, in this case I use it because it illustrates best my meaning. So that we are going to say now

Unemployment Continuance Act
that we shall not pretend that the act has expired on a certain date. It is not pretence to say that the act expired because we all know that it expired at the time stated. That is, therefore, illogical, and is bad grammar. But we can pretend, or assume that it did not expire. I think it would be better if it read as follows:
The orders in council and regulations made thereunder shall be deemed not to have expired, etc.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The language of many statutes by custom and habit is not always the language that purists and stylists such as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) would choose. In this instance the law officer of this house has settled the terms in the manner indicated and I think there is sufficient authority in British statutes of a similar character for the use of the words in just that way.

Mr. Chairman, I had not finished my observations. The item which I mentioned and which appears at the bottom of page 65 covers repairs to a public building in Sherbrooke. I would direct the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that by the use of this method we will not be able to show the Canadian public a true picture of affairs for the next twelve months. I claim that that $742 should have been an expenditure of the Department of Public Works chargeable to income, such as is shown in the estimates or provided for in the contingent fund. Had this been done, the Auditor General's report for next year would show the expenditures for public works as so much, and the expenditures for unemployment as so much. Using this method more money will be shown as having been expended on unemployment than really was legitimately chargeable thereto, while the phblic works estimates will show a smaller expenditure than was actually the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should realize that this was not an ordinary expenditure nor was it intended to be such; this is an expenditure of $742 to cover repairs to that building for one purpose and one only, to afford relief and employment. It does not rank with the ordinary expenditures for public works. All the safeguards with which the law surrounds expenditures are observed by the Auditor General and by the departmental officials, and I am quite sure that the minister in charge will be pleased to show to the hon. gentleman the original documents which refer to this expenditure. I cannot see that an expenditure thus made for a specific purpose

can be taken as having an effeot upon the general position of the country. It is regarded as money borrowed, and, as a matter of fact, it is part of the obligations of the country as a whole. If conditions improve, as we believe they must or else this country will not be worth even its loans, these obligations will be met out of income as they mature. We are thus enabled to transfer to income charges which ordinarily, but for the depression, would have been made against income.

That may be all right as far as it goes, but surely the Prime Minister does not think that when the city of Sherbrooke is spending $320,000 on unemployment, an expenditure of $742 will change the situation very much?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

That is just the point. I do not think a correct picture of the nation's affairs will be shown in the future. I do not doubt that vouchers can be produced for the money expended, but I do not like this way of doing things. I contend that this expenditure for repairs to the public building in Sherbrooke should have been chargeable to income or to the contingent fund, rather than to the unemployment fund.

to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister a matter which I mentioned last year. I told my right hon.
friend that I would not trouble him with details but I felt that the administration of the act should be looked into. At that time I had under my hand the particulars of a number of instances in which I felt that the money of the country was being wasted in so far as it was not reaching the needy and

Unemployment Continuance Act
those for whom it was intended, and that others were being discriminated against. I wanted to give my right hon. friend and the Minister of Labour a chance to evolve some system whereby there would be a decent and proper distribution of labour. A few days ago I mentioned that the system had not proven, at least in the province of Nova Scotia, to be working out in the interests of those who are most in need.
I shall mention three or four instances to my right hon. friend, and I believe that he as a business man and as a man who intends to get the most for the country's money in the way of relief will realize that these instances indicate that this money is not being properly spent and is not reaching those for whom it was intended.
One case was brought to my attention in my own constituency where of those employed on the work, three were in good circumstances, four had bank accounts, and ten were unmarried men. There were several men with families in that neighbourhood who were in hard circumstances but who were refused work. I do not intend to put on record the reason for this refusal, but I will say that it was not that they did not need work. I do not believe that the Minister of Labour himself would approve of the reason given and that is why I ask for an investigation of some of these cases.
Another case was where one man employed on the work was well enough off to be able to lend money to the school section, while the only support of a widowed mother was refused work.
In another instance the son of a widowed mother of eight, the bread winner of the family, three other men each with five or six dependents, one with a family of nine and ten others were refused work while there were employed one man with a bank account, and an unmarried man whose father and brother were both permanent employees of the provincial government and had been working steadily.
In another instance where seven men were employed, no less than five had bank accounts, while others, in need were refused work.
I have received a return in connection with another case at lower Sandy Point in Shelburne county. In this instance the total expenditure was $2,996, one thousand dollars of which was unemployment relief money. The gentleman employed as foreman was a storekeeper, the owner of an automobile and the operator of a taxicab. He drew no less than $229 at the rate of $4.50 per day.

This money was all spent together and I cannot tell where the one begins and the other ends. The foreman on this work where $1,000 of unemployment relief money was expended was a storekeeper. In addition to this, two of his sons were employed. One drew $99, and the other $110. That makes about $438 out of the $2,900, or nearly half of the $1,000 drawn by these three men.
In addition to that, another shopkeeper who was on the work, a Mr. Coffin, appears as a labourer and as a timber man and appears also for a team of oxen, and a gentleman who I understand is his son appears for a double team, and they between them get $340. So there is a total of $778 paid out to men who did not need unemployment relief at all, $778 out of a total vote of $2,900. Now if that situation exists generally, then it seems to me that we are not getting the benefit of the unemployment relief money and that it is not being devoted to the purpose for which it was voted by this parliament or which was intended by the government; for the government did make definite regulations that party and creed and religion and race was not in any way to interfere with a man's employment. But that has been allowed to interfere in connection with these cases and in connection with quite a number of others that I could cite.
I have not brought this matter to the attention of the committee without first having brought it to the attention of the Minister of Labour, not my hon. friend who now occupies that portfolio (Mr. Gordon), but his predecessor. I wrote to his predecessor

Unemployment Continuance Act
last fall and gave him one of these instances and asked him to investigate the case. I also wrote to the director of unemployment in Nova Scotia and called his attention to the matter. The then Minister of Labour wrote me back that it was something of a minor case; that was the adjective he used. I wrote back rather strongly and intimated that it seemed to me that the government was not doing its duty and the Department of Labour was not doing its duty if it did not see that this money reached the people for whom it was intended, namely, the needy, and that nobody else but the Minister of Labour and the Department of Labour were responsible for seeing that this money reached this class of people. We had some correspondence about it, but the result was nil. Now those instances have occurred and they still remain uninvestigated.
This is what I ask of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. I ask, first, that these cases be investigated. If the information which is given me is wrong I want to know it, but this is the information that comes to me, and I believe it to be correct. The information has come from a number of different sources which I believe to be reliable.
I ask, in the second place, that some method be adopted by the Minister of Labour, who is responsible for the administration of this money, whereby the selection of the unemployed will be made by people who have no political interest one way or the other, such as the overseers of the poor, the clergymen of the district, a Red Cross committee. Somebody who knows who are those most in need and who are most deserving, should be selected for the purpose of saying who shall go on these jobs; for I say to my right hon. friend, whether he thinks it is the case or not, that down in Nova Scotia in a great many cases the needy' and the unemployed are waiting outside the doors of the Tory patronage committee to see if they are going to get put on the job or not, and men are being taken on just under the same old organization as operates in respect of ordinary federal public works. That is, a foreman is appointed, a friend of the party. He meets the patronage committee, and they decide who is going to get the work and who is not, and they are influenced in very large degree by the politics of the various applicants. I say it cannot be otherwise so long as my hon. friend the Minister of Labour leaves it that way. All the instructions that he can issue and all the orders in council that he can put through will not stop that sort of thing, because after all what you are trying to do, or should do,

is not to deal with the matter here in Ottawa, but to reach the needy of that particular district and provide them with work and an opportunity for sustenance for themselves and their families. The people who are allowed to make the selections are in many cases not taking the instructions issued from Ottawa. So I ask my hon. friend in the first place to investigate, and in the second place to adopt a different system in regard to the distribution of these relief moneys and particularly in the selection of the men who are to receive this relief work.
I wish to deal with certain other questions.

Would it not
necessarily happen in cases of the kind to which my hon. friend has referred, that the selections would be made by the officials of some municipal government?

No, not in the counties
I know. I only wish that were true. The selections are made in the instances to which I have referred, I am informed, by the usual district patronage committee, the political patronage committee in the district.

Is my
hon. friend quite sure of the facts, or are his statements merely hearsay? He is a lawyer and he knows that the evidence which he has given to the committee would not for one minute be received in a court of law. It is a hearsay statement. I venture to say that the selection of these officials, if it is done in the same manner as it is done in New Brunswick, is made through the provincial government. In every case an outstanding man in the community is selected as foreman to take charge of the work. He will be a good man in whom the public will have confidence. The storekeeper to whom my hon. friend referred, if he has given a correct statement of the facts, and I am not questioning that at all, probably is a man who understands construction, and the fact that he runs a little country store does not preclude him from being capable of carrying on construction work of that character.
It means that other people who are just as well qualified and who need the work do not get the job.

That mayor may not be true. I am pointing out that being a storekeeper does not necessarily mean that he is not a proper man for carrying on that work. I venture to suggest that if the facts were known it would be found that the foreman was appointed through the provincial

Unemployment Continuance Act
Department of Public Works, the municipalities in these cases not having anything to do with the employment of the men and not contributing anything.

If my hon. friend will
listen to me, the foreman is appointed on the recommendation of the district engineer for the federal Department of Public Works. Because I was frank enough to say that I would like to have an investigation, my hon. friend seems to think that I am not quite convinced of the soundness of the case I am presenting.

I do not
say that.

What I say and what I
said before is that I received my information from a number of different sources which I believe to be reliable, and when I state that according to the information a storekeeper is selected for work of this kind and that men with bank accounts in different places in the constituency I represent are being put on the work, I say that the burden is on my right hon. friend to have an investigation and find out who is making these selections, because the men selected and given the work are not the men for whom the money was voted at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman said that the district engineer made the recommendations.

I know that the district
engineer made the recommendations, but of course he made them on the recommendations of the local patronage committee. That is what he always does.

That is
what he did when you were minister.

Certainly he did, and I
am not making any objection to that system when you are dealing with ordinary federal public works. I have never objected to that system in the case of ordinary federal public works. I have taken my medicine, if you like to put it that way, and when I have been administering patronage people have been selected who have been favourable to the government. But that is not what we are dealing with here. We are dealing with relief to the needy. The Prime Minister stated so himself. He said that the relief of the needy is what we are after. Under these circumstances you cannot have the same system that prevails under what is known as the ordinary political patronage system. That is what I am saying. I say to my right hon. friend that
so long as you use the ordinary organization, with the local district political patronage committee selecting the foreman, and the foreman consulting with the committee to find out what men he should put on the pay-roll and what men he should not, you cannot have a fair administration of the act.

Is the method followed in Nova Scotia any different from that followed in the other provinces?-in Quebec, for instance, where the municipalities alone select the men upon whom these moneys are to be spent, and by whom the work is to be done?
I have never heard in my constituency of the municipalities making any selection of that kind whatsoever.
Is not the work done by the municipalities?

No. The work is either direct federal public work or work contributed to by the provincial and federal administrations. I know of no instance where the work has been municipal. When my right hon. friend has that machinery he cannot expect it to work properly. There would be no use having the most .pious regulations in the world. Therefore I submit he has to revise his method and select some sort of impartial committee, or the overseers of the poor, or a citizens' committee. I wrote to the provincial director of unemployment, Mr. Spicer, and made that suggestion to him. I said, "Get the services of the overseers of the poor; they know the poor and those who need work. They are the people to make selections. Or, if that is not satisfactory, let the Red Cross or a local citizens' committee do the work." He wrote back and said he did not think-
Get a good Liberal.

Well, if we had one or two Liberals out of ten or twenty it would not be so bad. I assure hon. members opposite that even some of the Liberals are needy. I made the suggestion to Mr. Spicer and he wrote back saying he was not sure that the men suggested by overseers of the poor would be the best for the work. I assure you, Mr. Chairman it is better to spend unemployment relief money for those who are needy even though some might not do as efficient work rather than for those who do not need assistance.
What kind of work was it?

Work on breakwaters,
wharves and roads. '

Unemployment Continuance Act

I know I should not interrupt my hon. friend but I should like to ask what portion of the relief moneys in the province of Nova Scotia is expended on wharves and breakwaters such as he has suggested? I should like to ask this further question: Is it not true that 97 per cent of the foremen appointed by engineers in Halifax responsible for the construction of the breakwaters were appointed by a Liberal administration? Is that not so?
Mr. Chairman, shall we return to the question before us?
I should like an answer.

I do not know how much money was spent on wharves and breakwaters. The minister may be able to tell my hon. friend. I should think that in the western end of Nova Scotia about $50,000 has been spent on wharves and breakwaters.
I want to tell my hon. friend that this government spent $148,000 in the constituency represented by my hon. friend.

I have a return in my room. I am not going to bandy words with my hon. friend, but I assure him he is wrong. With regard to the appointment of federal engineers I must say I do not know whether any have been appointed lately or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are appointed by the Civil Service Commission.

I do say that in our district the recommendations to the engineers are made by local committees. With that machinery we cannot get along very well, so far as the administration of these funds is concerned My hon. friend the Minister of Labour should see that the situation is remedied.

The situation which has
been spread upon the record by the hon. member, if true or based upon facts, would of course raise great anxiety anywhere in Canada. It is strange, however, that the Department of Labour has never received a single complaint, even from the hon. member himself.

I am surprised at that
statement. If the minister had ever read his files he would know something about it.
I do know.

He knows nothing about
it.
You are in Montreal, and not in the Department of Labour.

My hon. friend will find
a file of his own predecessor setting out specifically one instance, and adding that the instance described was but a sample. A further request was made that the then minister make an investigation.

Instead of sending a
sample why did you not send the substance?
My hon. friend has made one statement which has proven to be wrong. During the last day or two he has shown a lamentable lack of knowledge of the working of his department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A very unfair statement.

He would have done
better to have stayed in the house and listened to the discussion than to run around the corridors, as he has been doing.
Very small, cheap.

My hon. friend got up
and made the statement that I had not made a single complaint, when the fact is that I had expressly stated before and repeat it today that I had made complaints. There are available about four letters which passed between the predecessor of the present minister and myself. Why does he take that stand? Simply out of ignorance, that is all-nothing else.
Oh, oh.
Getting nasty again.

In view of the fact that
complaints have been made, will the minister have investigations made? If he finds that my contentions are correct, will he take steps to correct the mistake and have selections made by some body capable of selecting men for these different works? I wait for the minister's answer.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member does not need to wait long. I have had something to do with the administration of the act, and for the past two years have worked in conjunction with many bodies throughout Canada. I am not going to suggest mistakes have not been made. Owing to the fact, however, that my hon. friend lives in the city of Montreal, far away from his riding, and his information is purely hearsay, I do not feel inclined to have investigations made.

Unemployment Continuance Act

That is about the finest
exhibition of shifty work I have witnessed.
You should know.

I have given my hon.
friend the facts. I have been in my own constituency, and talked with the men who gave the information to me. My contentions are on record in the department over which my hon. friend has control. However, if he is quite content with it-
Give us the names.
Yes, let us have the names.
The minister is not interested in them, at all.
Yes, I am quite interested.

I believe the Minister
of Public Works wishes to make a few comments.

Mr. Chairman,
I desire briefly to reply to some of the statements made by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). I wish to assure him that when starting out on this program to relieve the unemployed the government and every member of it kept in mind the primary object of having the work conducted in every case so as to provide the largest possible measure of relief to those in need. I think my hon. friend will admit we had no easy task, and that at times it is impossible to conduct work of this kind in a way which will be absolutely fair and satisfactory to all parties concerned. We agree also that sometimes for some motive or another complaints are made which are not well founded. Sometimes the motives are political, and sometimes they are motives equally unsatisfactory. I wish to assure my hon. friend that from the beginning the Department of Public Works and the officials connected with it have realized their responsibility. We started out with the fixed determination that as far as we could control the situation the work should be given to those who most needed it. I am not aware that my hon. friend sent to the department any complaints whatever with respect to work in his constituency. If he did, such complaints were immediately investigated, and if any abuses were found they were corrected -not only in his constituency, but in every other constituency from which any complaints came.
From the beginning the government has made a sincere and honest, and, in large measure, a very successful effort to meet the unemployment situation in the administration
of these works. I am going to read to my hon. friend a letter that early in the season was sent out from the Department of Public Works to all the district engineers. It is dated November 25, 1931:
Dear Sir,-
It has, in a few instances, been reported to the department that the spirit and intent of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, in connection with employment of labour, have not been fully lived up to. The purpose of providing funds from which works would be carried out was to give employment to the needy and this was to be so arranged that the funds available for payment of labour would be distributed as fairly as possible among those in the locality where work was being carried on who were known to be in need, and in the first instance to those who were also the support of dependents.
Employment was to be given to parties in the above category regardless of political affiliations, race or creed.
The department wishes to reiterate that employment is to be distributed as fairly as possible among the people in the locality where money is being expended by giving employment to those in need of funds to sustain their dependents and themselves, and who have not other resources to carry them over the present period.
Employment is to be offered regardless of any political or religious affiliations, or racial stock.
In order that employment may be distributed amongst the needy as fairily as possible, the authorities in the locality who are in a position to know the circumstances of heads of families, and who can be most relied on to furnish a list of parties in need, are to be consulted, and the men are to be engaged in rotation for a few days at a time.
You will be expected to see, as far as possible, that the spirit and intent of parliament in granting the funds for this purpose, and of the government in allotting the funds, are met.
Kindly let me know what your procedure is in assuring this result.
That letter on the instructions of the head of the department was sent by the chief engineer to every district engineer. We have many letters of approval and commendation as to the way in which the works have been carried on. As I have said, any complaint that came in was immediately investigated. In some cases foremen were suspended, in other cases they were dismissed, and in every instance a sincere attempt was made to rectify anything that was not in keeping with the spirit of this legislation and with the tenor of these instructions.
The minister will admit that his orders were not always obeyed, then.
In some instances they were not, and, as my hon. friend said, in his constituency where they were not obeyed the conditions were very speedily rectified.
Unemployment Continuance Act
Was a copy of that excellent letter sent to every Conservative member and to every defeated Tory candidate?
No. This is a letter of instructions to the responsible officers of the department-the district engineers-and it meant just what it said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) not only wrote Mr. Spicer, who under the Department of Labour was the director of expenditures under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, but he also wrote to myself, and I was at pains to take up direct with Mr. Spicer the question which he raised in his letter. I am extremely sorry that not knowing that this stage of the subject would come under discussion this afternoon I am at the moment unable to place my hands on the answers I received and the statistics I have with respect to the investigations I made. But I am in a position to say this, that in every one of those cases investigation was made, and the information which came to me was that these works with respect to which my hon. friend was complaining that his friends were not being employed in as large numbers as they ought to be, were direct public works, which are entirely different, as my hon. friend will know-
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -from relief works as such. Furthermore, my hon. friend in his statement a few moments ago said that the foremen in question were appointed by the district engineer of the Department of Public Works at Halifax. If that is so, it is evident upon its face that they were direct public works.
Oh no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Otherwise the appointments in question would come under the direction of the Department of Labour upon the recommendation of the representative of the Department of Labour in Nova Scotia.
But let me say this to my hon. friend. Although I have not the records before me, I know something of political divisions in that province, I know something of the political atmosphere down there, and speaking from memory, but I think with correctness, I may say my hon. friend was the only member from Nova Scotia who wrote to me by way of complaint with respect to expenditures in tha-t province. Furthermore, let me say to him that his complaint arises in the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth. I hope the fact that that is the only constituency from which at the moment I have had complaints of any

kind whatsoever does not cast any reflection upon the character of the political administration carried on there when my hon. friend was minister. But the fact of the matter is this, his are the only complaints I have had from that province. On the other hand, I have had numerous complaints from political friends of my own that they were not getting opportunities for employment, and they presented upon the face of it a very good case indeed why they ought to be employed. They complained very bitterly that a large number of Liberals could get employment.
But to my mind the best evidence upon the whole that expenditures in that province were based upon unemployment and need, irrespective of the political affiliations of those who were employed, is found in the circumstance that the Halifax Chronicle-which I may say is a rock-ribbed, thick-and-thin Liberal newspaper, the like of which is not to be found in any other part of Canada- sent a reporter down through the province to investigate expenditures upon public works, and amongst other places, he visited the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth. I am sorry I have not under my hand-if the debate proceeds beyond to-day I will produce it- the statement in that newspaper by its reporter that he found the work had been distributed with absolute fairness so far as the political complexion of the people employed was concerned. My hon. friend is too wise to attempt to argue from the particular to the general, but in effect that is what he is trying to do w'hen he cites the case involving some S200. Let us admit that in the case in point men who should not have been employed were employed. I submit that this proves nothing in view of the fact that there was authorized for the province of Nova Scotia, not only under the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act but through direct public works, the expenditure of no less than $1,600,000, the larger part of which was either expended or in process of being expended. As my hon. friend knows, a large part of that amount was spent on highways under the direct supervision of the province, which made a contribution. I may say to my hon. friend that I have yet to receive one complaint from the province of Nova Scotia that this work was not fairly allocated and divided without regard to the political views of the men employed.
I would say this:	If my hon. friend has
no better evidence with which to bolster up his assertion that money was improperly expended in Nova Scotia than the evidence he has brought forward this afternoon-if it

Unemployment Continuance Act
can be called evidence-then he has made a very poor case indeed. I submit that in all fairness to my hon. friend. I think in justice not only to the provincial government but to this government, with regard to expenditures which were made by the Department of Public Works, it is only fair that I should make this general statement in reply to my hon. friend.

As my constituency joins
that of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth, I am somewhat familiar with conditions in that part of the province. Perhaps I know a little more about those conditions than the hon. member knows, because I spend a great deal more time among my constituents than he spends among his.
I had some $56,000 of this unemployment relief money expended on public works in my constituency, and the only complaint I heard was that too many Liberals and not enough Conservatives were obtaining employment. The trouble with my hon. friend is that his constituency has been Liberal almost constantly since confederation, and a Conservative never obtained a single dollar of public money that was spent in that riding. The Liberals have been so accustomed to spending public money that when a Conservative gets a few dollars they think it does not belong to him, and that is the whole difficulty.
The Minister of Finance mentioned the Halifax Chronicle, which sent a reporter around to the different works to see how the money was being spent. I hold in my hand a report that appeared in the Halifax Chronicle, and every Liberal in the province of Nova Scotia swears by that paper whether it is right or wrong. This article refers to one of the public works undertaken in my constituency, and it states:
Public wharf at Weymouth is completed.
Four hundred foot wharf costing $15,000 built entirely from 'local labour unemployment aid.
Weymouth, February 5.-The public wharf built at Weymouth North during the late autumn and winter under the unemployment relief work act is now completed. The wharf which is 400 feet long was built under the supervision of Captain H. B. Fitzgerald of Weymouth North,-
I may say that Captain Fitzgerald is also a storekeeper. My hon. friend mentioned that a storekeeper had been acting as foreman. Captain Fitzgerald is a storekeeper, but previously he was a ship builder and he is thoroughly competent. I assume that the man in my hon. friend's constituency is the same type. Many of these men are retired captains who built vessels in their day, and
who are familiar with carpentering work of that kind. The article goes on:
-and was of great help to the people of that district who had no employment. It gave work to about 100 men, fishermen, farmers, labourers -regardless of politics or religious creeds. The men worked in shifts with about twenty-three men to a shift; besides the work on the wharf itself, the getting of timber and lumber also gave employment to the nearby mills in the getting and sawing of it.
Further it states:
Practically the whole amount was spent in this place, the money for iron for the piers was spent in Digby county.
I quote this article in order to show that as far as work in my constituency was concerned, the foremen were instructed by the district engineer to give employment to as many persons who needed it as they possibly could, regardless of politics, religious views or anything else. It seems very peculiar that in the constituency of Shefcume-Yarmoutih, which adjoins mine, there should be so many complaints. As I say, I never received a single complaint except that too many Liberals and not enough Conservatives were receiving employment.
I'll bet you fixed that.
No, I did not; I am not such a dyed-in-the-wool politician as my hon. friend. Every man in my constituency got a square deal.
Oh, yes! !

This refers to only one of the federal works carried on in my constituency. The men were employed in shifts, twenty-three men to the shift, and over 100 men were given employment in that way. Probably another fifty men were kept busy getting out timber, ballast and supplies of that nature. This principle applied to every undertaking in my constituency; I visited each one personally and know whereof I speak. I am speaking from personal knowledge; my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth is speaking from hearsay, which he gets from party politicians in the different places where work is proceeding.

In the first place, I am not taking the investigation of the Halifax Chronicle, as my friend the minister calls it, one way or the other; I am bringing to the attention of a responsible minister the fact that on the information I have-and I can give the names of the specific works-the order in council has been seriously violated in respect of the men who are receiving the benefit of this money. I do not care whether or not in Digby county there is a single example, but

Unemployment Continuance Act
I am rather surprised at the minister when he says he has not heard of any complaints. If he had read the Chronicle as much as he professes he would have seen a number of letters from men all over the province complaining very bitterly of the fact that they were deprived of work because of their politics.
That was not on public works; that was on highways.

I remember distinctly a letter from a shore fisherman at Arichat, a man with twelve children, who complained that he was told "You want relief work now. You were so smart; you voted against us and prevented your women from coming to the polls in my car." That was in the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, and that letter appeared in the Chronicle. It is rather extraordinary that it escaped my hon. friend's attention.
I am not concerned with the matter of the Chronicle; I am concerned with the fact that in this constituency there are these instances coming to my attention of people who did not need unemployment relief half as much as their neighbours needed it, but who got that relief while others were deprived of it. The ministry can do as they like about it, but 1 ask them to investigate that condition, I say to the Minister of Finance that the only suggestion I have heard of any investigation made by Mr. Spicer was one instance, in which the best he could say was that all the men employed on the work were those who previously had been unemployed. That has nothing to do with the case. There are many men worth millions who are unemployed, but that does not entitle them to unemployment relief money. My point is that those most in need were not getting the work, and that aspect of the case does not seem to have been met. My hon. friend says he has looked into the matter; I appreciate that. But since he did look into the matter he might have given me the benefit of Mr. Spicer's report in connection with it. This is the first I have heard of his having made a report. I am appealing once more to the ministry, and if it is the Minister of Public Works I am delighted to take his assurance, because I understood it was the Minister of Labour who had to do with furnishing the work. I understood that the Minister of Public Works was the one actually doing the job, the mechanic, if I might put it that way with deference, although the people to be selected were necessarily the wards of the Department of Labour. That, I should think, would be the chain of responsibility. If the Minister of Public

Works will look into the matter I am perfectly satisfied that his investigation will be a fair one. Will the ministry give me that assurance, that they will look into these various cases to which I have referred? Surely I am not going to be expected to bring affidavits when I give specific instances in the constituencies. W'hen I point out that there is this complaint, surely the ministry of its own motion will make investigation without anything further. I do not have to come and prove the case here. I am not acting as prosecutor at all; I am simply bringing the matter to the attention of the ministry and asking them to investigate it.

So far as I recall, my hon. friend has not disclosed the names of the places where this work has been done. If he will give the names of the places and write a letter giving the substance of the complaint I will see that the matter is investigated.
Progress reported.
